args.name: coldstart_save_default_highscore

args.name: set_sprite_shadow_xy_and_msb
args.comment: X (masked to 0-7, then +1) selects a sprite. Stores zp $08 to dat_1F50+X and zp $07*2 to dat_1F40+X (shadow copies, not the real $D000 sprite registers -- probably built once per frame and blitted to hardware elsewhere so sprites do not tear mid-raster). Carry out of the ASL (i.e. bit 7 of the un-doubled value) sets or clears one bit of a 2-byte table at dat_1F9C, built via a shift-loop rather than a lookup -- the classic idiom for a sprite MSB/multicolour/priority register shadow, but I have not traced dat_1F9C to $D010 to confirm which VIC register it shadows.
Immediately follows the RTS ending set_sprite_shadow_xy_and_msb; disassembles cleanly as 6502. Forcing decode -- likely reached the same way (indirectly / by a caller elsewhere not yet traced).

args.name: raster_irq_handler

args.name: reserved_9FEF_BFFF
args.comment: Sampled the whole span with read_bytes in 8192-byte chunks: $A001-$BFFF (8191 bytes) is uniformly zero. args.name: sid_note_freq_lo
args.comment: Low byte of a SID voice-1 frequency value, indexed by X = a note number read from a note/duration byte stream via LDA ($13),Y at $88F7 (loc_88F7 is a music sequencer: reads note at Y=0, duration/flag at Y=1 checked against terminator $F0, advances the 16-bit pointer $13/14 by 2 per step). Paired with sid_note_freq_hi at $89CD -- two parallel arrays (lo table, hi table) rather than one interleaved record, so add_type (which declares fields within one element) does not fit this shape; recording the pairing in these two comments/names is the workaround.

args.name: sid_note_freq_hi
args.comment: High byte of the SID voice-1 frequency value for the same note index X as sid_note_freq_lo at $898C (STA V1FREQLO / STA V1FREQHI at $88F7). Values rise roughly exponentially ($02..$54), consistent with a chromatic-note frequency table.

claims.name: bank_copy_ptr_tbl
claims.comment: Read by sub_5007 (LDX from zp $02, then LDA dat_502F,X / LDA dat_5030,X to build a source pointer, then copies 2048 bytes to $0800-$0FFF). Only 1 byte of dat_502F and 11 of dat_5030 are visible in this gap; if read as (lo=dat_502F[X], hi=dat_5030[X]) with X stepping by 1, dat_5030 bytes 10,00,18,00,40,00,48,00,50,00,58 look like six little-endian 16-bit source addresses ($0010,$0018,$0040,$0048,$0050,$0058) rather than six separate lo/hi pairs looked up by a doubled index -- but this is read from the shape of the copy loop, not confirmed by seeing a caller set X, so treat the exact indexing scheme as unresolved.

claims.name: msg_beasts_remaining
claims.comment: HUD line, decodes (screen-code) to a string ending in BEASTS REMAINING, one non-letter glyph byte, then a trailing 0. The trailing 0 is presumably overwritten at runtime with the live beast count.

claims.name: msg_stand_by_player
claims.comment: HUD line, decodes to STAND BY YOUR BEAST, one non-letter glyph byte, then PLAYER ONE. That same glyph code is reused in msg_beasts_extinct and msg_enter_your_name below. The trailing ONE is patched to TWO for player 2 by suffix_two_patch_a, copied by sub_5143.

claims.name: suffix_two_patch_a
claims.comment: Copied by sub_5143 (LDX#3; loop LDA suffix_two_patch_a,X / STA dat_05AE,X / DEX / BNE) over the tail of msg_stand_by_player's copy in the work buffer when zp location cur_player == 2. Only bytes 1-3 (TWO) are actually written; byte 0 (a space) is never copied since the loop stops at X==0.

claims.name: msg_beasts_extinct
claims.comment: HUD line, decodes to YOUR BEASTS ARE EXTINCT, the same non-letter glyph byte, then PLAYER ONE. Same ONE/TWO patch mechanism via suffix_two_patch_b.

claims.name: suffix_two_patch_b
claims.comment: Same mechanism as suffix_two_patch_a at $51C0, duplicated here for sub_53EC's copy of msg_beasts_extinct instead of msg_stand_by_player.

claims.name: msg_enter_your_name
claims.comment: HUD line, decodes to ENTER YOUR NAME, the same glyph byte, then PLAYER, then ONE at offsets 24-26 and TWO at offsets 27-29 back to back. Unlike the two messages above, this one bakes both suffixes into the same table; the caller at loc_561E picks which 3-char window to read by adding 3 to the starting index when cur_player==2, instead of patching after the copy.

claims.name: kbd_char_table
claims.comment: Values 0-1A (screen-code A-Z), then space, two more codes, then FF as a sentinel. Read by sub_5695 as kbd_char_table,X after X is found by scanning kbd_scan_table for the current LSTX value -- X is a shared index into both tables; this one gives the character to return.

claims.name: kbd_scan_table
claims.comment: 31 raw CIA keyboard scan codes (from LSTX / $C5), same length and same index space as kbd_char_table at $56AE. sub_5695 loops X 0..31 comparing LSTX against this table; a match at position X yields kbd_char_table[X] as the typed character. This is the keyboard-scancode-to-screen-code relation behind the name-entry screen (see msg_enter_your_name).

args.name: tbl_8A0E_unresolved
args.comment: Tail of the $898C-$8A3B span, right before loc_8A3C. No absolute-address reference found into this span. Bytes: 03 13 21 16 0F 09 25 1B 07 12 20 19 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 02 0B 06 07 08 03 04 06 07 09 03 08 05 0A 07 09 03 01 07 03 05 04 06 00 54 57 4F. Small values throughout, several short ascending runs (03 04 05 06 07 08 09 appears twice) -- guessing a further small table (durations? note-stream data reached only through the $13/14 pointer this project has not traced to an initial value?) but not confirmed. Last 3 bytes read as ASCII "TWO" -- possibly incidental, possibly the tail of a nearby string this claim's extent cut into; worth re-checking if $8A3C's neighbourhood changes.

args.name: player1_state
args.comment: Per-player save area, 128 bytes. Selected (alongside player2_state at $5F80) by cur_player in sub_5359/sub_539B, which swap it with the live screen row + zero page $58/$50/$54 so a split-screen two-player game can keep each side status separate. Seeded at cold start ($8A3C) from dat_90F8 for the first 40 bytes.

args.name: player2_state
args.comment: Same shape as player1_state at $5F00. First 40 bytes seeded at cold start ($8A3C) from the same source (dat_90F8) as player1_state; a separate 4-byte field at +8 (offset $5F88) is seeded from dat_8A38 by the loop right after.

args.name: cur_player
args.comment: Zero page selector, seen compared against 1 and 2 (sub_539B, msg suffix patching) and against 2 alone (sub_5359, loc_561E). Chooses between player1_state/player2_state, and between the ONE/TWO suffix in msg_stand_by_player, msg_beasts_extinct and msg_enter_your_name. Zeroed once at cold start ($8A3C); where it is set to 1 or 2 has not been traced yet.

args.name: wave_anim_frames
args.comment: 16 frames of 8 screen-codes each (indexed as frame*8+column by loc_8E74/loc_8E9A: X = frame_index*8, then 6 of the 8 bytes per frame are copied to dat_1FF0,Y, one column at a time). Screen codes $20 (blank) and $26-$2A (5 distinct glyphs) trace out a peak sliding left-right across the 8 columns and rising/falling through the 5 glyphs -- a wave/pulse animation, most likely the moving indicator I saw named NEUTRONIUM STATUS in hud_status_text ($90E4). Frame selection depends on zero-page $22/$23 (compared against #$03), not yet traced further.

args.text: Copies 2048 bytes ($0800-$0FFF) from a source selected by bank_copy_ptr_tbl ($502F/$5030), indexed by X = zero page $02 as set by the caller before the JSR. Destination is fixed. Looks like a bank-switcher swapping some 2K asset (font or HUD graphics bank) into a shared work area; see the comment on bank_copy_ptr_tbl for why the exact table layout is not pinned down.

Progress in 5xxx: found a shared per-player mechanism -- zp $0056 (named cur_player) selects between two 128-byte state blocks at $5F00/$5F80 (typed PlayerSlot), and between ONE/TWO suffixes in three HUD strings (msg_stand_by_player, msg_beasts_extinct, msg_enter_your_name). Also a default 4-entry high-score table at $5474 (typed HighScoreEntry, 52B/entry, 208B total -- matches the size of the $5E00 buffer your C0xx LOAD/SAVE writes, almost certainly its seed data) and a keyboard scancode->char pair of parallel tables (kbd_scan_table/kbd_char_table at $56CD/$56AE) behind the name-entry screen. Moving to the $5848-$87FD gap next, then the big $0801-$4FFF span which looks like one large sprite sheet (rendered several chunks -- camels, aliens, digits, no code reaches it yet).

args.name: tbl_bounce_0123210
args.comment: 6-entry symmetric ramp (0,1,2,3,2,1) read by LDA dat_9259,X in loc_9206 and stored to dat_2148,Y in a 16-iteration loop -- a triangle-wave index table, the same idiom as wave_anim_frames at $8DF4 but shorter and numeric rather than glyphs.

args.name: tbl_96F7_range_lo
args.comment: Read by sub_96D2 (CMP dat_96F7,X then CMP dat_96F8,X, X from zp $5F) as two overlapping bytewise arrays one offset apart -- looks like a per-index (lo,hi) range test, e.g. is LSTX ($C5, the last key scanned) between dat_96F7[X] and dat_96F8[X]. dat_96F8 overlaps already-decoded code one byte to the right, so its own extent was not separately claimed.

args.name: pad_before_filename
args.comment: 53 zero bytes then $40 $3A ("@:"). SETNAM only reads the 16 bytes at $C102 (highscore_filename), so this "@:" is not part of the name actually used -- reads like the start of an unused/alternate KERNAL replace-save prefix (@0:NAME convention) that never got wired up, or simply coincidental bytes. Not confirmed.

args.name: pad_after_filename
args.comment: 10 bytes of $FF then 3 zero bytes, filling out to the end of the runtime image ($C11E). Unreferenced; plausible assembler end-of-segment fill.

args.name: patch_arm_countdowns
args.comment: Self-modifying-code patcher, called once from loc_9D59 ($9D99). Overwrites the OPCODE byte (not the operand) at 7 addresses inside other routines, always to a mutating form: dat_9C22/dat_9EEA/dat_9FBB <- $C6 (DEC zp, target stays $4A), dat_9E68 <- $99 (STA abs,Y, target dat_043C), dat_9FB0 <- $9D (STA abs,X, dat_043C), dat_9EB8 <- $DE (DEC abs,X, dat_043C), dat_9C12 <- $FE (INC abs,X, dat_043C). Paired with the opposite patcher at $C046 (patch_freeze_countdowns), which overwrites 5 of these 7 same addresses with non-mutating opcodes ($A5 LDA zp / $B9 LDA abs,Y / $BD LDA abs,X) -- same operand bytes, different opcode, so the surrounding instruction's addressing mode and operand are reused unchanged and only the verb (DEC/INC/STA -> LDA) flips. Guess: a shared piece of per-object update code is toggled between "really tick this object's counters" and "just look, do not change" -- e.g. attract-mode/demo vs real play, or a pause. Not confirmed by tracing what calls $C046 (no absolute-address caller found -- likely reached the same indirect way as the sprite routines at $8B5F).

args.text: Opposite of patch_arm_countdowns ($C023): overwrites the same opcode bytes at dat_9C22/dat_9EEA/dat_9FBB/dat_9E68/dat_9C12 with non-mutating equivalents ($A5/$A5/$A5/$B9/$BD, all LDA). Does not touch dat_9FB0 or dat_9EB8, which patch_arm_countdowns also sets -- those two stay whatever they were last armed to. No absolute-address caller found for this routine.

3.name: score
3.description: seven PETSCII/ASCII digit characters, all zero in the shipped default table

14.name: message
14.description: flavour text, space-padded to the field width. Stored as plain PETSCII/ASCII (0x41-0x5A for letters), unlike the screen-code HUD strings elsewhere in this file (dat_511B etc, which use 0x01-0x1A for letters) -- corrected after an initial char(38,screen) declaration rendered this field as line/card-suit graphics instead of text.

args.name: obj_type
args.comment: One byte per object slot (X, up to at least 16 slots -- sub_8B20 zeroes 16 of them at init). Holds the type/kind index of whatever occupies slot X, written by spawn_object_from_template ($9772) as TYA;STA dat_1D10,X right after copying that type's template fields. Read back all over the object-AI code ($9744,$97CB.. through $9C6B) as LDA/LDY dat_1D10,X to fetch Y = type, then Y indexes a further per-type table (e.g. dat_1DF8,Y) -- a two-level indirection: object slot -> type -> per-type property. This is the central "one thing refers to another" relation in the game logic.

args.name: spawn_object_from_template
args.comment: X = target object slot, Y = template/type index (from sub_C061 -> sub_9DBB). Copies one byte from each of ~10 per-type template arrays (dat_1DA8,Y / dat_1DB0,Y / dat_1DB8,Y / dat_1DC0,Y / dat_1DE0,Y / dat_1DE8,Y / dat_1DF0,Y / dat_1DF8,Y / dat_1E18,Y / dat_1E20,Y) into the matching per-instance arrays at offset X (dat_1FB0/dat_1D30+dat_1F70/dat_1D40/dat_1D50/dat_1D60+dat_1E70/dat_1D70+dat_1E80/dat_1D80/dat_1D90/dat_1F60/dat_1E90), then stores Y itself into obj_type,X. The template tables are separate parallel byte arrays (not one interleaved record), so add_type (fields-within-one-block) does not fit this shape -- documenting the pairing in these comments is the workaround.

args.name: plot_char_and_color
args.comment: Writes A to screen via ($48),Y, then adds #$D4 to the pointer's high byte ($49) -- turning a screen-RAM pointer ($04xx-$07xx) into the matching Color-RAM pointer ($D8xx-$DBxx, since colour RAM = screen + $D400 -- $04+$D4=$D8) -- and writes a second byte (from $05) as the colour at the same offset. X (compared to #$28=40) looks like a column bound check. Called from many places (16 refs); the closest thing this program has to a print-character-with-colour primitive.

args.name: tramp_9DBB
args.comment: One-instruction trampoline (JSR sub_9DBB; RTS) living in the small $C0xx block alongside the LOAD/SAVE and self-modifying-code patch routines -- this block seems to be used as a fixed, easy-to-JSR anchor point rather than calling sub_9DBB directly from spawn_object_from_template.

args.text: Nice, that explains something I flagged as a guess: sub_8A42 ($8A42-$8A61) copies the same masked byte to dat_5F00,X AND dat_5F80,X for X=0..39 during init -- that is initializing both PlayerSlot copies identically, matches your cur_player finding exactly. My area ($88D4-$C11E, $9FEF-$BFFF) is now fully covered in find_undecoded (0 remaining spans on my side). Highlights: raster IRQ handler at $88D4/$88D5 (JMP into a 703-instruction per-frame routine at $8BC9); a SID note frequency table split lo/hi (sid_note_freq_lo/hi at $898C/$89CD, 65 notes) read by a music sequencer (loc_88F7) via an indirect note-stream pointer; an animated 8x16 wave/pulse glyph strip (wave_anim_frames at $8DF4, confirmed by render -- looks like a moving peak, probably the NEUTRONIUM STATUS meter); a two-level object system -- obj_type,X ($1D10) tags each of >=16 object slots with a type, and spawn_object_from_template ($9772) copies ~10 per-type template arrays (dat_1DA8 etc, indexed by type Y) into per-instance arrays (indexed by slot X) -- classic slot->type->property indirection, could not express as one add_type record since the fields are separate parallel arrays rather than one interleaved block; a self-modifying-code pair (patch_arm_countdowns $C023 / patch_freeze_countdowns $C046) that overwrite opcode bytes (DEC/INC/STA <-> LDA) at up to 7 addresses elsewhere, same operand, to toggle 5-7 spots between mutating and read-only versions of themselves -- likely attract-mode vs real play. $9FEF-$BFFF is genuinely empty (all zero after 18 stray bytes), not a decode gap. $5848-$87FD is still open if you want a hand once you finish the sprite sheet.

args.name: obj_behavior_jumptable
args.comment: Low/high byte pairs (interleaved: dat_9933,Y = lo, dat_9934,Y = hi), read by sub_993A: Y = 2 * (dat_1FB0,X AND $7F) -- a per-object value with its top bit masked off, doubled to a word index. Result stored to $02/$03, then JMP ($0002) at $994C. 3 entries decode to real routines: Y=0 -> $9939, Y=2 -> $994F, Y=4 -> $99C0 -- so this is a behaviour dispatch: an object's low-7-bits-of-dat_1FB0 value selects which of (at least) 3 update routines runs for it. I had first force-decoded these same 6 bytes as code (AND/STA/RTS) before finding the real reader at $9933 -- reverted.

args.name: obj_behavior_and_flag
args.comment: Per-object-slot byte (indexed by X, same slot numbering as obj_type at $1D10). Bit 7 is tested alone in several places (e.g. sub_9413: AND #$80) as an on/off flag; the low 7 bits, masked with AND #$7F, are doubled and used as the index into obj_behavior_jumptable ($9933) by sub_993A -- so this byte packs a flag and a behaviour selector together. Same AND #$7F / AND #$80 packing shows up on dat_1D60 and dat_1DF8 too -- a recurring one-flag-plus-7-bit-value convention across several of these per-object tables, not something the model here has a bitfield vocabulary for beyond this comment.

claims.name: opt_header_options
claims.comment: Section header on the title/options screen: OPTIONS

claims.name: opt_wave_sequency
claims.comment: decodes to WAVE SEQUENCY then a non-letter glyph byte then NORMAL. Plotted unconditionally by sub_5216ish; the glyph is the same kind of decorative byte seen elsewhere (values above the A-Z/space/digit range).

claims.name: opt_players_1
claims.comment: decodes to PLAYERS then a glyph then 1. Only plotted (at $525B onward) when zero page $59 is set -- a second options row shown conditionally.

claims.name: opt_random
claims.comment: decodes to RANDOM. Companion label to opt_players_1, same conditional block.

claims.name: opt_distance_between_zones
claims.comment: decodes to DISTANCE BETWEEN ZONES then a glyph then 00. The trailing two-digit field is a BCD-ish counter at dat_05B0/dat_05B1, stepped by 2 (wrapping 0-20 back to 7) by sub_5300 when key scancode 6 (LSTX==6) is pressed on the options screen -- this is the difficulty/spacing setting, zero page $57 holds the raw value that dat_05B0/05B1 render as decimal.

claims.name: msg_pause_mode_on
claims.comment: HUD line: PAUSE MODE ON, then space padding, then ANY KEY RESTARTS.

claims.name: unresolved_5870_block
claims.comment: Not understood. Read as plain ASCII/PETSCII it contains recognisable 6502-mnemonic-shaped fragments -- STA $07F7,X / RTS / TYA / PHA / AND #$07 / SEC / TAY / INY / LDA #$00 / ROL A / DEY / BNE -- interleaved with bytes outside printable range, so it is neither clean text nor anything this reading could place a shape on. Recorded as a plain data span rather than guessed at further; flagging this honestly instead of inventing a structure for it.

claims.name: audio_table_pause
claims.comment: Two short tables of small paired bytes (roughly duration/value pairs), each ending in F0 FF 00 FF, then zero padding out to $5A00. Shape consistent with a short two-voice tune or sound-effect script (e.g. for the pause jingle heard nearby), but the exact field meaning was not traced into the SID-writing code that would confirm it.

claims.name: credits_scroll_text
claims.comment: Long scrolling text block, ending exactly at $5E00 (the high-score save buffer). Opens WELCOME TO REVENGE OF THE MUTANT CAMELS / THIS PROGRAM WAS WRITTEN OVER A TWO MONTH PERIOD BY JEFF MINTER / THE INTRODUCTORY MUSIC WAS ARRANGED FOR TH[E...] and continues from there -- this confirms the game title and author from the bytes themselves. I already knew both facts about this real game before this reading; recording that here rather than presenting it as a bytes-only discovery. Not transcribed further by hand past the opening lines; 1024 bytes is a lot of scrolling prose and the point of this claim is coverage, not a full transcript.

args.text: Correction/addition: on the title-options screen (around $525E-$528D) this same location is toggled 0/1 with INC + AND #$01 to highlight a 1 PLAYER / 2 PLAYER choice, and is read as a plain zero/nonzero flag at $525E. So it holds 0/1 here but 1/2 once a game is running (sub_5359 etc compare it to 1 and 2). Either the menu writes 1/2 before starting the round, or there are two related-but-distinct uses of the same byte across game phases -- not confirmed which.

args.name: raster_split_dispatch
args.comment: Entered from the raster IRQ (raster_irq_handler_body, $88D5) on every raster interrupt. Dispatches on zp $1E (a phase counter, reset to 0 in the phase-3 arm below, otherwise not seen incremented in this routine -- the IRQ handler only does INC $1E before jumping here, so $1E cycles 0,1,2,0,1,2..): phase 1 sets the next raster split at $D8 and re-derives SCROLX from $1F; phase 2 sets the split at $F8, turns on the top of the display (clears SCROLY bit7) and rounds SCROLX down; the fallthrough (phase 0 / anything else) is the heavy one -- reads sprite-sprite collision (SPSPCL->$44), arms the next split at $90, calls sub_96D2 (a special-key check gate) and conditionally sub_508B, then runs a second, separate counter at $1F (0..7) that round-robins per-frame housekeeping: score/HUD countdowns at $2A/$29, a wrapping scroll counter at absolute dat_1F70 (not the per-object array of the same address -- a real address collision, not an alias), the wave animation trigger (JMP loc_9206) on count 4, and a table walk over dat_0630 on the rest. I decoded and covered all of this (no undecoded bytes remain in it) but did not chase every branch target to a name -- covered, not fully understood in the sense the brief means for the class of "say what things are made of".

args.text: Great finds, especially the self-modifying patch pair and the slot->type->template indirection (that is exactly the kind of relation this run is about -- worth a comment on obj_type,X and the template arrays even if it cannot be one record). I have finished 5000-5847 (options/title-menu screen: player count, wave-sequence mode, distance-between-zones difficulty, high-score table + name entry + keyboard scan table, per-player state swap) and just claimed $5848-$5DFF (pause message, an unresolved ASCII-fragment block I could not explain, two small audio tables, and the WELCOME TO REVENGE OF THE MUTANT CAMELS / JEFF MINTER credits scroll -- I already knew the game title and author in the real world, flagging that rather than pretending it was a cold discovery). Since 9FEF-BFFF turned out empty, if you have room: please take $5848-$87FD (still open, likely more game logic given your object-system work borders it at $87FE/8A3C) and I will do the big $0801-$4FFF sprite sheet, which is a visual-inspection job best done by one person. Shout if you would rather swap.

My area is done. Going to start helping on $5848-$87FD since it's still open -- will begin at the low end ($5848) and work up, posting before I go deep on anything so we do not overlap if you are also circling back to it.

claims.name: msg_here_we_go
claims.comment: decodes to HERE WE GO then three copies of the same non-letter glyph byte (0x51) then padding -- likely three exclamation-style decorative glyphs in this custom charset.

claims.name: msg_well_done
claims.comment: decodes to WELL DONE then a glyph then YOU HAVE SAVED CAMELKIND then the same glyph again then padding -- end-of-game congratulation message. The glyph (0x54) is yet another of the non-letter decorative bytes seen throughout this file (0x51/0x52/0x54/0x56 so far), consistent with punctuation drawn from a redefined character set rather than the standard A-Z range.

claims.name: msg_cheat_mode_operative
claims.comment: decodes to CHEAT MODE OPERATIVE, space padded both sides.

args.name: seed_highscore_buffer
args.comment: Nothing calls this in the code reached so far, hence the missing root -- but it is unambiguous: LDX#0/LDA#$20/STA $5E00,X/INX/BNE fills all 256 bytes of $5E00-$5EFF with spaces, then LDA highscore_entry_1,X / AND #$3F / STA $5E00,X for X=0..207 copies the 208-byte default high-score table (highscore_entry_1..4 at $5474) into it, converting each byte from PETSCII/ASCII (the table encoding, letters 0x41-0x5A) to screen-code (0x01-0x1A) by masking the top two bits. This confirms, rather than just size-matches, that $5474 is the seed data for the $5E00 buffer the C0xx routines LOAD/SAVE as ATTACK MUTANT.HI.

args.text: Before I go further into $5848-$87FD: the live highscore buffer at $5E00 is the SAME 52-byte HighScoreEntry layout you typed at $5474 -- confirmed by finding entry boundaries exactly 52 bytes apart. It also has a hidden easter-egg default name in screen codes: "I LIKE CAMELS REALLY" for slot 1. Since you already own the HighScoreEntry type id, want to claim $5E00 (4 entries, 208B) as records of it yourself? I will steer clear of $5E00-$5EFF and pick up from $5F00 or further up instead so we do not step on the same type.

args.name: sprite_sheet_main
args.comment: placeholder - will replace comment next

args.text: One large sprite sheet, ~288 standard 64-byte hi-res C64 sprites (24x21) back to back, from $0801 to $4FFF -- nothing in the code reached so far references it (no root existed before this claim; find_instructions on the VIC sprite-pointer range $07F8-$07FF and on STA $D000-$D010 turns up nothing yet, and it explicitly reports several indirect/computed-address writes it cannot resolve, so the code that actually points the VIC at a sprite number almost certainly lives in the still-undecoded $5E00-$87FD span). Visually (rendered in 16-wide grid chunks): recognisable camels in several walk/leg positions, small flying/aircraft-like enemies, falling parachute figures, devil/pitchfork and skeleton figures, a robot, the digits 0-9 and some letters, and a band roughly a third of the way through that renders as visual noise in this hi-res view -- possibly debris/explosion-particle sprites that are just genuinely busy-looking, possibly something not meant to be read as a plain hi-res sprite (multicolour mode, or a different frame boundary); not resolved. Could not tie any specific sprite index to a name (camel/enemy/digit-N) because the selecting code has not been found yet -- recorded only the visual grouping, not an index mapping.

14.name: message
14.description: same field as HighScoreEntry.message, but this copy is screen-code (0x01-0x1A) rather than PETSCII/ASCII (0x41-0x5A) -- it is written by seed_highscore_buffer ($545C) via AND #$3F over the PETSCII source at highscore_entry_1..4, and is what gets POKEd straight to the screen and LOAD/SAVEd as ATTACK MUTANT.HI

args.name: live_highscore_1
args.comment: Live high-score slot 1 in the LOAD/SAVE buffer -- this is the one C0xx actually persists. Confirmed 52 bytes/entry, same layout as HighScoreEntry at $5474 but screen-code encoded (see seed_highscore_buffer at $545C).

args.name: live_highscore_2
args.comment: Live high-score slot 2.

args.name: live_highscore_3
args.comment: Live high-score slot 3.

args.name: live_highscore_4
args.comment: Live high-score slot 4.

args.text: Done -- claimed live_highscore_1..4 at $5E00 with a new type HighScoreEntryLive (same 52B layout, but message field is screen-code not PETSCII since seed_highscore_buffer converts via AND #$3F). Also a tooling note for both of us: find_undecoded does NOT seem to treat is:record claims as clearing a gap -- my 4 highscore_entry_N records at $5474 still show up as a 208-byte undecoded span even though claims_at and read_disassembly both show them fully fielded. is:bitmap/text/data claims do clear the gap list fine. Worth mentioning in findings as a tool limitation rather than something either of us needs to fix.

0.name: duration
0.description: Frames/ticks to hold the note; small values (1-14 seen). Not confirmed against a tempo constant.

1.name: note
1.description: Index into sid_note_freq_lo/hi ($898C/$89CD) via the sequencer at loc_88F7. $F0 marks the end of a phrase/track (checked with CMP #$F0 at $8928).

args.name: music_track_1
args.comment: Pointer 13/14 is set to exactly 5FFE by sub_9170 before the sequencer at loc_88F7 runs. Verified (duration,note) pairs are plausible (duration under 20 hex, note in 20-45 hex or note=F0) up to offset 558 (622D); the next two bytes (80 F0) break that pattern and are followed by a run of 16 FF bytes -- likely a second tracks silence or header rather than more of this one, so extent stops there rather than guessing further. sub_9170 also sets a second pointer pair 15/16 = 631E, which read_bytes shows starting a similar-looking but not yet verified (duration,note) stream -- probably a second music track (title vs in-game vs game-over is a common multi-tune pattern for this kind of game) not yet fully bounded.

args.text: Closer look: this repeats a small record shape roughly every 8-9 bytes -- a $00 terminator, two mystery bytes, a literal X, two more mystery bytes, a literal 6, a space, then a short mnemonic-shaped ASCII fragment (STA/RTS/TYA/PHA/AND/SEC/TAY/INY/LDA/ROL/DEY/BNE) with no operand. Reads like entries of the form (something, something, label-text) rather than raw code or a plain message. Not chased further -- would need to find what reads this table to know what the two mystery-byte fields are.

Wrapping up my side for now (0801-5DFF options/credits/sprite-sheet, plus the 5E00 live highscore records) and writing findings.md. Nice work on the object/template system and the raster IRQ + music sequencer -- that is a great relations example too. Will keep an eye on chat if you want a second pair of eyes on 5848-87FD.

args.comment: Already known as an entry point (called from loc_8A3C) but re-checking neighbourhood decode.

args.name: build_screen_row_ptr_table
args.comment: Builds a 40-entry (X 0..39) table of pointers to each screen row: dat_0340,X = low byte, dat_0360,X = high byte, starting at $0400 and adding $28 (40) each step -- the classic C64 screen-row-address lookup table, presumably to avoid recomputing row*40+col elsewhere.

args.text: Update on 5848-87FD: found the music engine data. sub_9170 sets the sequencer pointer (13/14) to exactly 5FFE and a second pointer (15/16) to 631E -- two separate tracks. Claimed music_track_1 (type MusicStep: duration u8, note u8, terminator note=F0) covering 5FFE-622D (280 steps, verified plausible byte-by-byte); the second track at 631E is very likely the same shape but I did not fully verify it. Also named build_screen_row_ptr_table at 87FE (the screen-row lookup table builder feeding into 8A3C). The rest of that span (roughly 6230-87FD, ~8.6KB) has no absolute-address reference anywhere I can find -- find_references and a spot-check of immediate-load high-bytes both come back empty, so whatever reads it does so through a computed pointer (like level-select-by-number) that I have not located. Small-value byte groups there (e.g. 83 81 01 87 82 83 at 6800) look like the same flag+7bit convention as the object tables, consistent with per-level/wave parameter data, but I am not confident enough to claim shape on it. Leaving it open -- flagging in my findings as coverage I could not close, not pretending otherwise. Also seconding your find_undecoded/record-claim note: my music_track_1 record claim did not reduce the undecoded count either, same limitation.

Posted findings.md in my working directory. Summary of what is now in the project from me: sprite_sheet_main (bitmap, 0801-4FFF), the options-screen text/tables (52C2-5359), HighScoreEntry/HighScoreEntryLive types + 8 records (5474 and 5E00), PlayerSlot type + player1_state/player2_state, kbd_scan_table/kbd_char_table, cur_player location, seed_highscore_buffer routine, and the 5848-5DFF messages/credits-scroll/audio-table/unresolved-block claims. Good luck with the rest of 5848-87FD -- ping me if a second pair of eyes helps.

Wrapping up on my side too -- findings.md written. My area (88D4-C11E, 9FEF-BFFF) fully covered; contributed the music tracks and screen-row table in 5848-87FD but left 6230-87FD (~8.6KB) genuinely open, no reference into it that I could find. Thanks for the collab -- the cur_player/PlayerSlot <-> sub_8A42 connection and the record-claims-do-not-clear-find_undecoded finding were both good catches on your side. Good luck with whoever writes the article.

args.name: boot-with-irq-shim
args.description: Boot the game with a 17-byte stand-in for the three KERNAL interrupt entry points this host has no ROM for: $FF48 (push and vector through CINV), $EA31 (KERNALs IRQ continuation, here just a jump to the exit) and $EA81 (pull and RTI). Nothing else of the KERNAL is supplied and the game body calls nothing else of it.

args.name: rng-walk
args.description: Same run as press-fire, but with 256 bytes of my own invention standing in for BASIC ROM at $A000-$A0FF -- the address sub_8D1D reads for randomness. This host has no ROM files, so without it the game's dice always read zero.

args.name: rng-zeros
args.description: The control for rng-walk: identical steps, but $A000-$A0FF left at zero, which is what this ROM-less host supplies. Same dice, every throw.
